newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS- T-bond volatilities deflate post-payrolls.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS- T-bond volatilities deflate post-payrolls.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options shrank, despite a steep drop in underlying bond prices, as risk premium was taken out after the release of December's U.S. employment report, dealers said.

"It pretty much always happens, almost no matter what," said a brokerage T-bond trader, referring to option prices' tendency to get pumped up prior to the monthly jobs data and then deflating on the actual news on the numbers.
Some big call sales in the Chicago Board of Trade bond pit as well as concerns over the weekend time-decay helped to depress volatilities, traders added.
Implied volatilties for CBOT February and March T-bond futures options sagged by about 0.3 point each to 9.6 and 9.8 percent respectively.

Among the biggest trades today, an investment bank was seen selling 5,000 contracts of March 112 calls and two houses were said to have traded a total of 7,000 legs of a combo trade, buying March 112 puts and selling 116 calls.
Early in the day, March T-bond futures tumbled on a stronger than expected jobs report and hit a low of 109-26/32, doun 1-19/32 on the day.

Non-farm payrolls jumped 262,000 against an upward revised 127,000 for November and average forecasts for a 192,000 increase. Hourly earnings rose six cents to $12.05 and the average workweek rose to 34.8 hours from 34.5 hours.
Traders said the numbers rekindled fears of a Federal Reserve credit tightening.
"It puts a negative spin on the whole market, but we'd kind of like to see Monday when everybody will have had the chance to let it all sink in," the brokerage trader said.
The March futures steadied after the big initial drop and have drifted in narrow ranges around 110 for most of the day.
In the Eurodollar pit at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, implied volatilities were also lower.
June and September implied volatilities were off about a quarter point each to about 12.8 and 15.4 percent.
"We're starting to see some interest at these levels, but the big event risk is out for now," an investment bank trader at CME said.
